Name: C Stuart Hardwick
Question: If evolution is not a sentient thing, how can it see colors? How can it know a rabbit in the snow needs to be white or a tiger needs to become orange to blend?
Answer: Evolution is not a force, a driver, a cause, or a plan, and it doesn’t “know”, “see,” “think,” or “foresee” anything. Evolution is the RESULT — the logically unavoidable result — of living populations producing varied offspring, not all of which survive equally. A rabbit that’s easier to find in the snow is more likely to be eaten and less likely to contribute the genes that colored its fur to the next generation. A tiger that’s easier to see in the bush and less likely to sneak up close to its prey, will make fewer kills, spend more energy on each kill, and contribute fewer genes to the next population. There is a great deal more in the details, but at its core, it’s just that simple.

Question: Why do nuclear reactors have to be so big?
Answer: Because you keep running the AC. Nuclear fission reactors do not have to be “so big.” This is the SNAP-10A nuclear fission reactor, thermoelectric generator, which generated 500 watts to power a series of military missile surveillance radar satellites in the 1960s. The reactor is the little can at the top, the rest is space radiator: This is the Kilopower KRUSTY reactor that is currently in development as part of a 1,000 watt thermoelectric generator for space applications: In both these reactors, heat is conducted across a thermopile to produce electricity, just like in an RTG, but the heat comes from a moderated fission reaction, not passive radioactive decay as in earlier RTGs. No shielding is needed until such a reactor is activated, and since it’s meant to be used in space and away from people, none may be needed there either. This is the CROCUS research reactor in Switzerland, which you can get the scale of from the labels: It generates no power and 100 watts of heat, and is used to produce neutrons and conduct experiments. It needs shielding to protect people from its radiation, but is simple and small and runs at low temperature with minimal risk to anyone. Small fission reactors are widespread, but they don’t produce much power. You need to run your AC, so we need something bigger. This is a modern naval reactor sealed inside the shielded containment vessel that will keep it safely away from people while in service and for long after. It generates 700 megawatts of heat, which will turn steam turbine producting something like 350,000 shaft horsepower and 125 megawatts of electricity. But you need to run the AC, so we need something bigger: This is the containment building for a new 1 gigawatt reactor under construction in Georgia, which will produce enough power to keep the AC humming in a quarter of a million homes. Name: C Stuart Hardwick
Question: Atheists always say they are backed by science, but can their science explain why it rains?
Answer: Imagine the sky as a giant sponge. This sponge can hold a lot of water vapor, which is like invisible water floating around in the air. When this sponge gets really full, it starts to wring itself out, just like when you squeeze a wet sponge. That's when it rains! Now, here's how it works: the sun heats up the Earth, especially water like lakes, rivers, and oceans. This heat makes the water turn into vapor—a gas—which rises up into the sky. As the vapor goes higher, it cools down and turns back into tiny water droplets. These droplets form clouds. This keeps happening until eventually, the droplets start bumping together and growing until they are too heavy to stay aloft and fall as rain. Ice crystals, dust, or soot (say, from a passing airplane) can seed cloud formation and accelerate the development of rain. Changes in temperature and pressure can vary the amount of water vapor the air can hold and so also influence the formation of clouds and rain. So, again in simple terms, rain happens when the air gets too full of water and the clouds can't hold it anymore, so they let it all out as raindrops. Rain that doesn’t evaporate runs off into lakes and rivers, trickles into underground reserviors, and eventually reaches the ocean. But sooner or later, water near the surface evaporates again and heads back up to the clouds. This is called the hydrologic cycle and is critical to life. An that’s just a little—highly simplified—of what science tells us about why it rains. Science, by the way, is just checking reality to see what’s true.

Name: C Stuart Hardwick
Question: What exactly is gravity? I understand its effects can be measured and predicted with extraordinary precision. But, what is the nature of the force. Is this one of those things that our scientists really don’t fully understand?
Answer: As far as we can tell, Einstein was correct in conjecturing that gravity is not a force in the sense of the other fundamental forces of nature, but rather the result of mass warping spacetime in such a way as to bend the forward motion through time of nearby objects. Yeah, I know that sounds like the sort of handwavium a science fiction writer would think up, but as far as we can tell—and we’ve looked experimentally with astonishing precision—this is literally, actually true: So, there you go. Gravity is no an attractive force, it’s just an apparent force that results when warped spacetime interacts with the inertia of objects drifting forward through time. Now, people will jump in the comments and claim that Einstein never said this, that it was only a mathematical convenience, and they will point to a letter in which he said something that sounds like that. This is absolutely not true. The letter in question is one Einstein wrote to Cornelius Lanczos on November 21, 1949 in which he said “Sie haben vollständig recht. Es ist verkehrt zu glauben, dass die 'Geometrisierung' etwas Wesentliches bedeutet. Es ist nur eine Art Eselsbrücke zur Auffindung numerischer Gesetze. Ob man mit einer Theorie 'geometrische' Vorstellungen verbindet, ist [unleserlich] Privatsache.” "You are completely correct. It is wrong to believe that 'geometrization' signifies something essential. It is merely a kind of mnemonic device for finding numerical laws. Whether one associates 'geometrical' concepts with a theory is … a matter of personal preference." Superficially and out of context, you can certainly be excused for thinking that that sounds like Einstein didn’t see spacetime as a real thing but merely a mathematical construct—but you would be quite wrong. Einstein’s point was not that spacetime wasn’t to be taken seriously as a real thing that exists, but merely that mathematically “geometrization” in general should not be assumed to reveal the whole trueth, and clearly this is correct. Spacetime is real, as far as we can tell, but no mathematical model of it we have ever devised is accurate and complete. Photons, electrons and Protons are real, but they are neither particles nor waves but weird things we call “quanta” that can have characteristics of each, despending on how we interact with them. Einstein was not saying spacetime isn’t real, he was expressing the limitations of even the best human tools in understanding the underlying reality around us.
